details:
What it does

Crew Health Monitor is a web app for a four-person crew on a long mission. Each morning a crew member confirms readings from simulated worn sensors (a smart shirt for blood pressure and pulse, a glucose monitor, a core-temperature headband and a wrist sleep tracker) or types them in by hand. The app checks each reading three ways: against published limits (AHA, ADA, CDC, AASM, NASA-STD-3001 and others), against the same person's last 14 days, and for slow drift since the mission started. The worst result sets the status to normal, watch or alert. Every flag says what changed, which line it crossed and where that line comes from, why it matters in space and what to do next.

One crew member is the Crew Medical Officer (CMO). The CMO sees the whole crew with the worst status first, can open anyone's dashboard read-only and can record exams. Every time the CMO views someone's data, it goes into an access log the crew member can see. An emergency guide covers chest pain and collapse, with CPR steps that change with gravity: the Evetts-Russomano or handstand method in weightlessness and kneeling CPR on the Moon or Mars. Every step is time-stamped, and the app builds a summary for the flight surgeon. A separate Mission Control console shows the crew's data in UTC, along with when each record would reach Earth. Reminders flag missed check-ins, which go to the CMO after 2 days and to the ground after 3. Short health activities (a reaction game, a breathing exercise and a shared exercise journey) earn mission patches for taking part, never for scores.

Why it matters

On a Mars mission the one-way signal delay can reach about 22 minutes, so the crew can't wait for a doctor on Earth. Space also shifts sleep, heart rate and bone health, so limits made for people on Earth can miss early changes. Comparing each person with their own baseline catches drift sooner, and the plain-language explanations help a CMO who is usually not a doctor.

How we built it

The app uses Next.js 15 and React 19, written in JavaScript, and is deployed on Vercel. Scoring runs in the browser and saves to the device first, so the app keeps working during a communication blackout. An optional onboard server (Supabase, Postgres) syncs records and re-scores them. Python scripts build every data file the app ships with, and over 380 automated tests cover the scoring logic. Our backend team also built a Java Spring Boot API for the next version. We used no physical hardware, so the sensors are simulated.

We tested the detection methods on real public data. On 253 nights from 47 adults on PhysioNet, the detector caught 83% of 12 bpm rises in sleeping heart rate with false alarms held near 5%. Grip-strength percentiles come from 13,393 adults in a Kaggle dataset, and the cabin checks use NASA's RR-1 data from the ISS. We tried an Isolation Forest and a population risk classifier as well, and dropped both because they caught fewer changes or couldn't explain their flags.

What we considered

Crew privacy, offline use, honest sources (any line we set ourselves is labelled "team-set" in the app) and the difference between gravity on a station, the Moon and Mars. The crew data is synthetic. The app is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
